 Inspiration 

 About ten years ago, I experienced a psychotic episode that led me to live on the streets and later to be hospitalized in a psychiatric hospital in Mexico City. My perception of reality had become erratic, and at the time I was told that medication might be something I would need for the rest of my life. 

 What followed was a very long process of rebuilding myself. 

 Meditation and activities that forced me to focus my attention became extremely important. Programming became one of them. I say this without exaggeration: software development became one of the things that helped me rebuild my life and my mental health. 

 For years afterward, however, I lived with an almost permanent state of anxiety. It gradually improved, but my nervous system still felt deeply unbalanced. 

 Around three years ago, that became physical. I developed a neurological problem diagnosed as Cauda Equina Syndrome . For several months I used a wheelchair and then crutches. I lost sensation in my feet and parts of my legs, and at one point I could not walk normally. 

 I eventually started a highly personalized Pilates rehabilitation program. 

 The difference was remarkable. I recovered my mobility, and today I am in what I consider the best physical and mental health of my life; I am not even medicated since many years ago😍. 

 That experience completely changed the way I think about exercise. 

 The strange part is that gyms still confuse me . 

 There is an enormous amount of information online about exercises, machines, routines, recovery, strength, mobility, nutrition, and health. But more information does not necessarily make the decision easier. 

 If I walk into a gym today, how do I know that a routine someone recommends is actually appropriate for me ? 

 Not for someone approximately my age. 

 Not for an average person with a similar goal. 

 For me — considering my history, current mobility, weight, previous injuries, preferences, progress, limitations, and whatever other relevant signals I choose to share. 

 This was the starting point for Adaptive World. 

 Interestingly, I had never seriously thought about building this product before the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. 

 The challenge made me think about WebMCP in a much broader way: 

 
 What if WebMCP eventually becomes a normal layer of web development, in the same way that SEO and accessibility (a11y) became normal considerations for websites and web apps? 
 

 Today a website explains itself primarily to humans and search engines. 

 A WebMCP-enabled website can begin to explain its capabilities to agents. 

 A gym could expose not only that it exists, but what equipment is actually available, what each machine can do, its specifications, what classes are offered, accessibility information, schedules, services, and other structured capabilities. 

 Then I asked the second question: 

 
 What if the agent could understand the person just as well as it understands the place? 
 

 That is the idea behind Adaptive World . 

 

 What it does 

 Adaptive World connects two types of context that normally live completely separately: 

 1. What a person needs 

 A private, user-controlled Digital Passport can contain relevant context such as goals, preferences, physical characteristics, mobility constraints, previous injuries, rehabilitation progress, wearable data, accessibility requirements, or other information the person chooses to make available. 

 It is intentionally not a profile that blindly exposes someone's entire medical history to every website. 

 The user owns the context and decides what can be used for a particular interaction. 

 2. What the physical world can offer 

 Businesses and physical environments expose their real capabilities through WebMCP . 

 For the hackathon MVP, that environment is a gym (and an OpenAI Showcase's website: https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/that I used it too in the demo). 

 The gym website exposes structured information about its actual: 

 
 Equipment and machines 
 Equipment specifications and capabilities 
 Classes and services 
 Rehabilitation or mobility options 
 Facilities and accessibility features 
 Other information an agent needs to understand what can actually be done there 
 

 The agent can then reason across both sides: 

 
 Personal context + real-world capabilities + feedback = an adaptive experience 
 

 Instead of asking an AI: 

 "Give me a gym routine." 

 I want to be able to ask: 

 "Given my goals, my history, my current condition, and what this specific gym actually has available, what makes sense for me today?" 

 That distinction is fundamental. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI can recommend exercises. 

 With WebMCP, it can reason about what is actually possible in the environment where the person will perform them. 

 For the rehabilitation scenario, the system can identify appropriate equipment and activities while respecting declared constraints, explain why they were selected, and clearly surface situations where professional guidance or medical clearance is appropriate. 

 And the interaction does not have to end when the plan is generated. 

 After a session, a person could record progress, discomfort, perceived exertion, mobility, completed exercises, or — eventually — automatically incorporate signals from a smartwatch or other wearable. 

 The next interaction can therefore start from a better understanding of the person than the previous one. 

 This creates a loop: 

 Understand → Match → Act → Measure → Adapt 

 

 How I built it 

 For the hackathon I intentionally reduced a very broad idea to one concrete, testable environment: a gym (+ Sunday Table website interaction https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/ ) . 

 The MVP models a gym website containing realistic equipment, services, classes, and machine specifications and makes those capabilities available to an agent through WebMCP. 

 Instead of asking the model to assume what a gym probably contains, the agent can discover the environment itself.
